title: Learning a Maximum Entropy Model for Visual Textures using Diffusion
claim: A two-branch network, with one branch conditioned on noise level and one on the noisy input, combines their outputs to predict the diffusion target.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right flow, two network branches merging at a dot product
description: A single wide block diagram. At left are three texture images: a clean stone-wall texture x, a Gaussian noise image ε ~ N(0, I), and a noisy texture y, with y's formula under it. The top branch sends x through colored feature-map stacks (purple, yellow, red, orange). These shrink in size and take a noise-level σ input through curved arrows. The branch ends in an orange vector λ(x,σ). The bottom branch splits y into two parallel UNet-style encoders with blue, purple, yellow and red stacks. Circled × symbols take inner products between corresponding channels at each scale. The resulting small colored vectors are concatenated into f(y). λ and f(y) meet at a circled dot-product node. That feeds a ∇_y node and then 'predict', which produces a noisy texture image at right, with the formula for v underneath. The colored stacks draw the eye first.
caption: Model diagram. The top and bottom networks compute vectors $\lambda(x,\sigma)$ and $f(y)$, respectively. Input and output images $\{x,\varepsilon,y,v\}$ are 128x128 in resolution. Blue, purple, yellow, red, orange colors represent channels with spatial resolutions 128x128, 64x64, 32x32, 16x16, 8x8, respectively (not drawn to scale). Top network is based on a ConvNeXt-T model [ref], and the $\lambda(x,\sigma)$ vector consists of spatial averages of channels at the last stage of the network. Bottom network is constructed from a twin pair of UNet encoders [ref], initialized and trained independently. The $f(y)$ vector consists of the inner products of corresponding channels in the two UNet encoders (for the final layer of each scale, just before downsampling). The gradient of the inner product of the two vectors provides an estimate of $v$ (see text).
abstract: Visual textures -- spatially homogeneous image regions containing repeated elements (e.g. a field of grass, the bark of a tree) -- are ubiquitous in visual scenes and provide important cues for recognizing and analyzing materials, surface geometry and objects. A number of existing texture models extract essential statistics from a single texture image, and can then generate high-quality samples that are visually similar to the original by matching these statistics. However, their statistics are either hand-designed or based on a network pretrained for another purpose (e.g., object recognition). Here, we develop the first principled method for unsupervised learning of a set of statistics that are used to constrain a maximum entropy probability model for texture. We leverage methods developed for generative diffusion models to derive training and sampling procedures, and compare these to the traditional method of sampling via matching the statistics. Despite the compactness of our trained model (512 statistics), it generates texture images whose quality is as good as or better than the current state-of-the-art model (~177k statistics), both visually and by quantitative perceptual scoring using DreamSim. Finally, we show that images generated from parameters lying along a line between the parameter vectors corresponding to two different reference textures are homogeneous textures with features that smoothly transition between those of the two references.
